a.text: Greg, I like the core insight here—there's real demand for home-cooked food and real supply from people who enjoy cooking but make too much or want extra income—but I think you need to pressure-test a few things before going further. Food safety and liability are the biggest risks: cottage food laws vary wildly by state and sometimes by county, so your subscription model could hit regulatory walls that a one-off marketplace (like a farmers market app) wouldn't face as acutely. I'd also push back on the subscription framing specifically—meal variety and cook availability are inherently inconsistent, so locking users into a recurring commitment might create churn and frustration if their "neighbor chef" goes on vacation or stops cooking that week. On the supply side, you'll need a compelling reason for home cooks to do this consistently rather than as a hobby, since the margins after your platform fee plus their time and ingredient costs may not be enough to retain them. That said, if you can nail a tight geographic pilot, solve trust/safety with reviews and basic health certifications, and test whether people actually want recurring meals versus on-demand ordering, there could be something real here—I'd just validate the subscription mechanic and regulatory landscape before building much more.
